info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 9.3: AI-Assisted Entity Tagging, Entity Linking, and Comparative Audit.

name.text: 01 Question: The AI Revolution in Philology: Flexible Models for Historical Prose

questiontext.text: Why are modern Large Language Models (LLMs) uniquely powerful for processing historical prose compared to older statistical taggers?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs bring deep semantic context and world knowledge to historical texts, surpassing the narrow window of traditional sequence taggers.

answer.text: Their billions of parameters capture rich contextual semantics, multilingual syntax, and world knowledge across centuries of textual history.

feedback.text: Correct. LLMs leverage deep contextual representations and vast multilingual pretraining to handle complex historical vocabulary and syntax.

answer.text: LLMs contain physical time-travel antennas that communicate directly with dead authors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs are computational language models trained on digital text corpora, not supernatural devices.

answer.text: LLMs are guaranteed to be 100% error-free and never require human review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs frequently hallucinate facts or syntax, requiring rigorous human verification.

answer.text: LLMs can only process text written in binary machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs process natural human languages fluently.

name.text: 02 Question: Why LLMs Excel at Historical Names: Semantic and Syntactic Depth

questiontext.text: How do LLMs overcome the boundary errors that plague statistical sequence taggers like SpaCy?

generalfeedback.text: Broad contextual attention allows LLMs to resolve complex entity spans and honorific titles without clipping.

answer.text: They model entire sentence structures and rhetorical discourse, recognizing that honorifics, titles, and multipart names belong to a single entity.

feedback.text: Correct. Global attention mechanisms allow LLMs to understand complex noun phrases and honorific formulas far better than local window taggers.

answer.text: They delete all titles from historical documents before reading them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs retain and analyze titles within their semantic context.

answer.text: They look up every word in a printed book using a robotic scanner.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs operate as digital neural networks processing token embeddings.

answer.text: They force every person's name to be exactly three words long.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs accommodate variable-length entity spans naturally.

name.text: 03 Question: The Hallucination Hazard: Inventing Plausible Fiction

questiontext.text: What is the 'hallucination hazard' when using generative AI for named entity linking?

generalfeedback.text: The hallucination hazard occurs when generative models invent plausible but non-existent identifiers or historical facts.

answer.text: The model confabulates plausible-sounding but completely fictitious Wikidata Q-identifiers, historical biographies, or citations.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative models prioritize probabilistic linguistic fluency and will invent synthetic URLs or Q-numbers if ungrounded.

answer.text: The model displays animated psychedelic graphics on the computer monitor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In machine learning, hallucination refers to confabulated or ungrounded factual claims, not visual graphics.

answer.text: The computer catches fire due to excessive processor heat.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hallucination is a semantic fidelity failure, not physical combustion.

answer.text: The model deletes all punctuation marks from the English language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation handling is unrelated to the hallucination of non-existent entity records.

name.text: 04 Question: Prompt Engineering: Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot Annotation

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a 'few-shot' prompt from a 'zero-shot' prompt in named entity tagging?

generalfeedback.text: Few-shot prompts provide concrete exemplary demonstrations, guiding the model toward strict schema compliance and boundary accuracy.

answer.text: A few-shot prompt provides curated input/output examples demonstrating the exact desired XML structure and edge-case handling before the test text.

feedback.text: Correct. Providing concrete demonstration examples anchors the model's output syntax and dramatically reduces structural errors.

answer.text: A zero-shot prompt costs ten dollars, while a few-shot prompt is free.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zero-shot and few-shot refer to in-context learning examples, not financial costs.

answer.text: A few-shot prompt can only run three times before expiring.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts can be executed repeatedly without limitation.

answer.text: A zero-shot prompt is written in Chinese, while a few-shot prompt is written in German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both prompting strategies can be authored in any language.

name.text: 05 Question: Injecting Editorial Policies: Positive and Negative Constraints

questiontext.text: Why must prompt templates include explicit negative constraints (e.g. 'DO NOT invent Q-identifiers')?

generalfeedback.text: Negative constraints explicitly block models from inventing fake identifiers when no authoritative record exists.

answer.text: Generative models are biased toward providing complete answers and will invent synthetic IDs to fill perceived gaps unless explicitly forbidden.

feedback.text: Correct. Negative constraints override generative confabulation defaults and enforce the Verified Absence rule.

answer.text: Because negative words make the computer processor run faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative constraints guide semantic generation; they do not alter hardware clock speeds.

answer.text: Because positive rules are forbidden by computer programming syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both positive and negative instructions are valid natural language constraints.

answer.text: To force the model to delete the text if an entity is missing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative constraints prevent fake data generation while keeping text intact.

name.text: 06 Question: Automating AI Prompts in VS Code: ai_entity_parser.py

questiontext.text: Why do scholars use a scripted Python runner (`ai_entity_parser.py`) in VS Code rather than manual interactive web chats?

generalfeedback.text: Scripted API execution locks in model parameters, ensures reproducible results, and preserves audit trails.

answer.text: A scripted runner ensures deterministic parameters (e.g. temperature=0.0), structured logging, repeatable execution, and version control.

feedback.text: Correct. Scripted pipelines guarantee reproducibility, parameter consistency, and automated integration into downstream audit workflows.

answer.text: Because web browsers are illegal for university researchers to open.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers are standard research tools, but manual chatting is non-reproducible.

answer.text: Because interactive chats automatically erase the user's hard drive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web chat interfaces do not erase storage devices.

answer.text: Because Python scripts cannot connect to cloud AI models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python is the primary programming language used to interface with AI APIs.

name.text: 07 Question: The TEI XML Schema Quality Gate

questiontext.text: What is the very first quality gate an AI-generated TEI XML fragment must pass before evaluation?

generalfeedback.text: AI outputs must pass schema validation first; malformed XML is immediately rejected as invalid.

answer.text: Well-formed XML syntax and strict TEI P5 Relax NG schema validation.

feedback.text: Correct. An output with unclosed tags, illegal attributes, or malformed nesting cannot be integrated into a scholarly edition.

answer.text: Conversion into an MP3 audio file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editions evaluate structured textual XML, not audio conversions.

answer.text: Approval by a commercial advertising agency.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commercial advertising has no role in scholarly XML validation.

answer.text: A spelling check against modern slang dictionaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts preserve archaic orthography and validate against formal TEI schemas.

name.text: 08 Question: The Token Alignment Gate: Matching Entity Spans

questiontext.text: Why is the 'Token Alignment Gate' essential when validating LLM predictions against the manual ground truth?

generalfeedback.text: The token alignment gate ensures the LLM did not silently alter, modernize, or drop primary witness tokens.

answer.text: LLMs may subtly rephrase, modernize, or drop words from the primary text, destroying direct token-for-token comparability.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative models occasionally 'clean up' or alter historical text; verification ensures the underlying witness tokens remain untouched.

answer.text: Because tokens in computer memory decay if not measured every five minutes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital tokens in memory do not physically decay.

answer.text: Because token alignment is required by the local electric company.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Utility companies do not regulate computational linguistics.

answer.text: Because non-aligned tokens cause the computer monitor to turn upside down.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Visual display orientation is unrelated to textual token indexing.

name.text: 09 Question: The Three-Way Comparative Diff in VS Code

questiontext.text: What three distinct tiers of data are compared in the Three-Way Comparative Audit?

generalfeedback.text: The Three-Way Comparative Audit contrasts manual ground truth, statistical NLP, and generative AI predictions.

answer.text: Tier 1: Manual Human Ground Truth; Tier 2: Deterministic/Statistical NLP (SpaCy); Tier 3: Generative AI (LLM).

feedback.text: Correct. The audit triangulates human expertise, statistical machine learning, and generative AI across identical text spans.

answer.text: Three different translations of the Bible into modern Spanish.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The audit compares three annotation methodologies on the student's primary witness.

answer.text: Three different web browsers running on three different operating systems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software browsing environments are not the subject of the linguistic audit.

answer.text: Three random files chosen from the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The comparison evaluates three structured tiers on the same manuscript excerpt.

name.text: 10 Question: Scoring the AI Pass: Precision, Recall, and F1-Score

questiontext.text: If an LLM identifies 18 entity spans correctly, misses 2 ground truth entities, and hallucinates 2 false entities, what are its Precision and Recall?

generalfeedback.text: Calculating precision (TP/(TP+FP)) and recall (TP/(TP+FN)) provides empirical accuracy metrics for LLM performance.

answer.text: Precision = 90% (18/20), Recall = 90% (18/20), and F1-score = 90%.
Precision = 50%, Recall = 100%, and F1-score = 75%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. With 18 true positives out of 20 predictions and 20 targets, precision and recall are both 90%.

answer.text: Precision = 100%, Recall = 0%, and F1-score = 0%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A model with 18 correct hits does not have zero recall.

answer.text: Precision = 10%, Recall = 10%, and F1-score = 10%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mathematical calculations must follow standard evaluation formulas.

name.text: 11 Question: Building the Three-Way Discrepancy Matrix

questiontext.text: What is the primary analytical function of the Three-Way Discrepancy Matrix in `ENTITY_AUDIT.md`?

generalfeedback.text: The Three-Way Discrepancy Matrix maps token-by-token consensus and divergence across human, statistical, and generative methods.

answer.text: To place Manual, SpaCy, and LLM annotations side by side for every disputed token, revealing exactly where and why methods diverge.

feedback.text: Correct. The matrix provides a structured, comparative view of consensus and divergence across all three methodologies.

answer.text: To calculate the monthly financial cost of running university servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The matrix evaluates linguistic annotation agreement, not server costs.

answer.text: To serve as a cryptographic key for encrypting credit card numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly matrices are analytical tables, not encryption ciphers.

answer.text: To list all books published in the seventeenth century.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The matrix focuses specifically on the excerpt under audit.

name.text: 16 Question: Auditing Entity Links: Detecting Invented Q-Identifiers

questiontext.text: What is the required verification procedure to audit an AI-generated Wikidata link (`@ref="wikidata:Q..."`)?

answer.text: Manually load the URL in a browser or query the Wikidata API to confirm the Q-number exists and refers to the exact historical entity.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholars never take AI links at face value; every URI must be verified against the live registry.

answer.text: Assume that if the number starts with 'Q' it must be 100% accurate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs frequently generate syntactically valid but non-existent Q-numbers.

answer.text: Ask the AI model a second time if it is telling the truth.

answer.text: Print the number on a piece of paper and bury it in the library.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly verification is digital, empirical, and transparent.

name.text: 17 Question: The Fallacy of Pure Automation

questiontext.text: What is the 'Fallacy of Pure Automation' in computational textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: The Fallacy of Pure Automation assumes machine models can replace human historical expertise without rigorous critical review.

answer.text: The mistaken belief that advanced AI models can completely replace human philological judgment and produce critical editions without expert review.

feedback.text: Correct. Automated models lack true historical consciousness and accountability; human scholarship remains indispensable.

answer.text: The belief that computers should never be used in university classrooms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital tools are valuable partners in research when guided by human expertise.

answer.text: The idea that steam engines are more efficient than modern electricity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Industrial history is unrelated to textual automation ethics.

answer.text: The claim that all historical documents were written by automated robots.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical witnesses were authored by human historical agents.
